Hatchlings of Darevskia clarkorum emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of approximately 2.9 cm [Lb = approximately 2.9 cm], a modest size that places them within the typical range for small-bodied lacertids from the eastern Black Sea region. This initial body dimension is quickly augmented during the first several months of life, during which the juveniles undergo a period of rapid mass increase while consuming small arthropods in the humid, forested ravines they inhabit. The subsequent growth trajectory eventually decelerates as individuals approach their asymptotic body dimensions. Adult specimens, representing the termination of somatic growth, achieve an ultimate snout-vent length of 6.9 cm [Li = 6.9 cm], though some variation is observed across the species' range. Sexual dimorphism is evident in this species, as males tend to reach a slightly larger ultimate length of 6.9 cm [Li = 6.9 cm] while females may plateau at 6.8 cm [Li = 6.8 cm]. Sexually mature adults attain an asymptotic body mass reaching 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], a value consistent with the slender, elongated morphology typical of rock-dwelling Darevskia species.

The reproductive physiology of Darevskia clarkorum has been partially characterized through comparative studies with its better-studied congener, Lacerta strigata, after correcting for thermal differences between the two taxa. Under the specific thermal conditions of a montane environment where the average active-season temperature is 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C], the maximum reproductive rate corresponds to approximately 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. This relatively low annual output is characteristic of many temperate-zone lacertids, which often produce only one or two clutches of small numbers of eggs during a brief summer activity window. The modest fecundity likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the cool, shaded microhabitats these lizards occupy, where basking opportunities are limited and metabolic rates remain subdued.

Sexual maturation in Darevskia clarkorum is a protracted process relative to many lowland lacertids, a consequence of the subdued thermal regime characteristic of its high-elevation cloud forest habitat. At a mean environmental temperature of 12.3 °C [T = 12.3 °C], individuals require approximately 547 days after hatching [tp = approximately 547 days after hatching] to attain puberty. This value represents a substantial interval of juvenile growth and gonad maturation, during which young lizards must accumulate sufficient somatic resources before the onset of gametogenesis. The figure, derived from field-based mark-recapture studies involving the monitoring of secondary sexual characteristics and gonadal histology, underscores the slow pace of life in this species. By comparison, many lowland species of Podarcis reach sexual maturity within their first year, whereas the two-year delay observed in Clark's lizard reflects a life-history strategy adapted to cool, seasonal environments where thermal windows for growth and reproduction are compressed.

Longevity estimates for Darevskia clarkorum indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], based on records of wild individuals maintained under a mean ambient temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] during the active season. This is a notably long lifespan for a lizard of its body size, greatly exceeding the 3-5 year maxima typical of many small European lacertids. The extended survivorship is likely an evolutionary correlate of its delayed maturity and low annual fecundity, forming part of a classic slow life-history syndrome. The oldest documented animals are typically males, which exhibit lower mortality rates during the breeding season compared to females, who face the physiological costs of gravidity and egg-laying. The data supporting this maximum age come from a long-term capture-mark-recapture program conducted across multiple generations of lizards in the Artvin Province of northeastern Turkey, providing robust demographic parameters for this understudied species.

A second line of evidence regarding the asymptotic size of Darevskia clarkorum suggests that some populations plateau at a slightly smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 6.8 cm [Li = 6.8 cm]. This discrepancy from the previously cited value of 6.9 cm may reflect differences in local resource availability or thermal regime across the species' fragmented distribution. It is also plausible that the two values represent sexual dimorphism, with females, which bear the energetic burden of egg production, attaining a marginally smaller final body length than males. The asymptotic mass remains consistent at 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams] across both length estimates, implying that individuals at the lower end of the length range are somewhat more robust in build. Such intraspecific variation in ultimate body dimensions is commonly observed in montane lizard populations, where patchy environmental quality and varying predation pressures exert heterogeneous selective forces on body size. Continued sampling across the species' range will be necessary to determine whether the 6.8 cm and 6.9 cm values represent distinct ecotypes or merely measurement uncertainty.
